extracted.intended_audience: design applicants, intellectual property practitioners, and policymakers interested in international industrial design registration
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, procedures and eligibility requirements for obtaining international protection of industrial designs through the WIPO‑administered Hague System (Hague Agreement / Geneva Act). Covers who may file, what must be included, fees, publication, examination, refusals, duration and renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized filing mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague system provides a mechanism for registering an industrial design in several countries by means of a single application, filed in one language, with one set of fees. The system is administered by WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single international registration can replace separate national filings in designated Contracting Parties; applicants should use the Hague system when seeking multi-jurisdictional design protection to simplify filing and fee payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable Acts / which instrument governs new filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Agreement consists of several instruments (1925 Hague, 1934 London Act, 1960 Hague Act, 1999 Geneva Act). As of January 1, 2025 the Geneva Act (1999) is the sole Act under which new international design applications can be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older Acts (London 1934, Hague 1960) have been frozen for new filings (London frozen earlier; 1960 frozen from January 1, 2025). Applicants must check which Act their target Contracting Parties are party to and file under the Geneva Act when filing new international applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification to use the Hague system
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants qualify to use the Hague system on the basis that: the applicant is a national of a Contracting Party; or is domiciled in a Contracting Party; or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in a Contracting Party; or has their habitual residence in a Contracting Party (habitual residence only available if the Contracting Party has adhered to the 1999 Geneva Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting Parties include intergovernmental organisations (e.g., EU, OAPI), so applicants domiciled in an EU member state that is not separately a Contracting Party may qualify via the EU's membership. An applicant who does not qualify under one of these headings cannot use the Hague system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application languages
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be filed in English, French, or Spanish, at the choice of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the filing language with attention to translation/communication needs; the language chosen is the language of the international registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application content and representations (views)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain one or more views of the designs concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear reproductions (views) of the design(s); these reproductions are what is published and examined by designated Contracting Parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and classification of designs per application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application can include up to 100 different designs provided that the designs are all in the same class of the International Classification of Industrial Designs (Locarno Classification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing multiple designs, ensure all designs fall within a single Locarno class; otherwise submit separate international applications. The 100-design limit is a hard cap per international application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee structure (basic, publication, designation fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application fee is composed of three types of fees: a basic fee, a publication fee, and a designation fee for each designated Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for all fee components; designation fees vary by Contracting Party. Fees are paid centrally to WIPO as part of the international filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal examination by the International Bureau (scope of WIPO review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application is examined for formal requirements by the International Bureau of WIPO, which provides the applicant with the opportunity to correct certain irregularities in the application. Once formal requirements are met, the application is recorded in the International Register and details are published electronically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO checks formalities only (completeness, fees, formal requirements). Applicants should respond promptly to invitations to correct irregularities to avoid delays or rejection on formal grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination and refusals by designated Contracting Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: If any designated Contracting Party considers that a design registered for protection in that Contracting Party does not meet its domestic criteria for registrability (e.g., finds that the design is not novel), it must notify the International Bureau that it refuses the registration for that Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive criteria (novelty, originality, etc.) are applied by each designated Contracting Party under its national law; applicants should assess national registrability requirements in designated countries and be prepared for possible refusals and corresponding national procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of no refusal (national effect of international registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every Contracting Party that does not issue such a refusal, the international registration takes effect and provides the same protection as if the design(s) had been registered under the domestic law of that Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a designated Contracting Party does not issue a refusal within its refusal period, protection is treated as a national registration in that territory; applicants should monitor notification and refusal periods per designated party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and deferral option
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard publication of Hague applications is 12 months after filing. The applicant can request either immediate publication, or delayed publication of up to 30 months. The Geneva Act introduced the option to defer publication for up to 30 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can defer publication for commercial or strategic reasons (e.g., to delay public disclosure while assessing markets). Consider national filing priorities and secrecy concerns when choosing publication timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of protection and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of an international registration is five years, extendable in further five-year periods up to the maximum duration permitted by each Contracting Party. For the 1934 London Act the maximum term was 15 years (historical). Renewals are handled centrally by the International Bureau; the applicant pays a renewal fee and notifies the International Bureau of the countries for which the registration is to be renewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renew centrally through WIPO rather than through each national office; however, maximum cumulative protection depends on each designated Contracting Party's domestic law. Keep renewal dates and fees tracked centrally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial scope and designation process
rubrics_metrics.description: An international registration takes effect only in the Contracting Parties designated in the international application; a list of Contracting Parties is maintained by WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select designations strategically (which Contracting Parties to designate) because designation triggers national examination/refusal periods and designation fees. Check territorial coverage (including OAPI/EU coverage) and any territorial limitations or extensions.
